items: Notice when your ideas get restated by your boss in meetings and the group responds only to their version — this pattern of idea erasure trains you to stop contributing.

Track moments when your boss presents your hallway suggestions to leadership as if they originated from themselves — this corridor attribution tactic is designed to make you doubt your own contributions.
Watch for situations where your specific work gets absorbed into 'team achievements' while your boss claims individual credit — this systematic misattribution is deliberate, not accidental.
Identify instances where your boss rewrites history about who originated an idea and then makes you feel petty for correcting them — this retroactive claiming makes you question your memory.
Write down exactly what you contributed, when it happened, and who was present — concrete details without editorializing keep your documentation objective and usable for future reference.
Keep a separate dated record of each incident outside company systems — using personal devices and email protects your documentation from being accessed, deleted, or denied.
Note your emotional state alongside factual details in your records — tracking how you felt helps you recognize patterns of manipulation and self-doubt over time.
Preserve emails, messages, and files that prove your original contributions existed — digital evidence creates an undeniable paper trail of your actual work.
Practice stating your contribution calmly in low-stakes moments first — rehearsing factual responses like 'as I mentioned in our one-on-one' builds your confidence without appearing territorial.
Set clear boundaries about what feedback is collaborative versus what is your individual work — having these definitions prevents your boss from retroactively claiming ownership of your ideas.
Decide on your escalation path before you need it — know whether you'll report to HR, your boss's manager, or your professional network so you're not deciding under pressure.
Recognize that fighting every incident will drain you — choose your moments strategically and preserve your energy for behaviors that cross clear lines rather than trying to correct every erasure.
